 Do not decide this by memory:
 
 ```bash
 keryx review blast-radius --ref "${BASE_SHA}" --previous blast-radius.json [--final]
 ```
 
 It prints the decision and the reason, and reuses the previous record when
 nothing moved. The final round recomputes whatever the file set did — otherwise a
 fix introduced in round 3 gets no regression check at all, and the round that
 certifies the flow is the one that checked the least.

-`keryx review readiness <review-id-or-path> [--json]` reads the package and prints eleven items, READY or NOT READY, each with the evidence and the command that repairs it.  1. `files-covered` — every changed file is in a wave or carries a recorded waiver.
 2. `blast-radius` — no file the blast radius cut is left unreviewed. A cut radius writes `chunks.json`; run `keryx review chunks plan`, `estimate`, `next`/`record`, `merge`. In an unattended run every wave runs without a question, up to the 25-pass ceiling; in an interactive run the operator is asked once: in keryx shell call `review_chunks_answer` (a card, never a terminal); elsewhere the operator runs `keryx review chunks estimate --package <dir> --answer yes --quote "<their words>"` in their terminal; unattended, record Not run.
 3. `reviewers` — every planned reviewer was dispatched and its result ingested.
 4. `verifier` — the verifier checked every finding it should, or the report says how many it did not.
 5. `ledger` — the ledger is READY.
 6. `coverage-md` — coverage.md does not list a reviewer as `run` that the dispatch record says did not finish. Re-run `keryx review ingest` for the package.
 7. `head` — the report's head is the PR head.
 8. `report-names` — pending mutation candidates and parity warnings are named in the report.
 9. `pr-files` — the changed-file count equals the PR's own file list. A recount more than 3x the recorded scope is refused: it came from the wrong base. Recount with `keryx review blast-radius --package <ref> --changed <the PR's files>`.
 10. `memory-outside-stage` — the orchestrator read memory only in its memory stage ("Clean context" above). Outside keryx shell it reads "not observable on this host" unless this session's keryx calls carry the caller token `keryx review start` printed.

Not waivable: each held finding needs its own answer, and `review_waive_readiness` / `--waive` refuse this item.
 12. `quotes-located` — every open finding whose quote `review ingest` could not place (absent from the file at the reviewed head, or in it more than once) has a disposition. Ingest keeps such a finding with no line, flagged `quote_unlocated` and listed in scope.md, instead of refusing the round. Re-quote one distinct line and re-ingest, record a disposition, or the operator waives the item.
 
 `keryx review complete` refuses status `completed` while any item fails. A failing item other than `premise-decisions` is waived only by the operator. In keryx shell call `review_waive_readiness` for the item: the operator answers it as a card, the waiver is recorded with the card text and the time, and then you run `keryx review complete`. Never send the operator to a terminal. Outside keryx shell the operator runs `keryx review complete --waive <item> "<their own words>"` in a terminal, repeatable. Unattended, record the item as Not run. `keryx review publish` is held by the same checklist. Publishing is the operator's decision too: in keryx shell call `review_publish` (a card shows the target and the body; never send the operator to a terminal). A not-ready package goes to GitHub only as a partial review (`review_publish` with `partial: true`, or `keryx review publish --partial`), which puts a "Partial review" header on the post and never approves. The shell guard stops a publish command that runs through the keryx shell; a publisher outside it (CI, another agent, a script file) is not stopped, and that limit is named, not hidden.
 
 ## Fix rounds — dispositions, regressions, withdrawal
 
 ### Every prior finding leaves the round with a disposition

later round cannot be screened against a set nobody recomputed.
 
 Do **not** write the record inside the package directory before the ingest. A round that names no `--review-id` has not allocated that directory yet, and creating it makes the ingest take the next free name instead.
 
 `--refuted` takes the findings this round **raised and then dismissed**, in the
 same finding shape, each carrying `disposition: {state, evidence}` with one of
 the `dismissed-*` states. Without it a package keeps only the survivors of an
 unlogged triage — which is why precision measured over the recorded corpus
 returns 100% whatever the reviewers actually got right.
 
 `review complete --finding <id> --disposition <state> --evidence <ref>` records
 what became of a finding when the fix round closes; the triple is repeatable, one
 group per finding. States: `unknown`, `acted-on`, `dismissed-incorrect`,
 `dismissed-wont-fix`, `dismissed-out-of-scope`, `dismissed-deprioritised`.
 Everything except `unknown` must cite where the outcome is written down — the
 commit, the test, the decision. A recorded state and its citation cannot be
 overwritten by a later close; record a correction as a new round.
 
 `review complete` on a PR-bound package refuses a merged PR or a moved head unless `report.md`'s first line names the reviewed SHA and says so; a package with no PR binding is unaffected.
 `review complete` refuses a report with no `Evidence level:` line (`static only — did not run: <what>` or `ran — <what>`); a package ingested before the field existed only warns.

 **Closing a fix round without dispositions leaves every finding reading `unknown`.** That is not "the reviewers were right"; it is "nobody wrote down what happened", and it is the single reason the precision figure cannot be read.

## Workflow
 
 ```
 review-premise Progress:
 - [ ] Step 1: Drop every finding below `minor`
 - [ ] Step 2: Per finding, read only its bare claim (title, file, quote) and the code there; form a view
 - [ ] Step 3: Collect intent signals at and around the site (see question 1)
 - [ ] Step 4: Answer the four questions
 - [ ] Step 5: Only now read the reviewer's problem, impact, evidence and suggested_fix; revise if they show something you missed
 - [ ] Step 6: Emit one premise claim per finding judged, and nothing else
 ```
 
 The order of steps 2 and 5 is the point. A reviewer's argument read first anchors the
 judgement on it; the claim and the code read first let you see what the reviewer did not.

 ## The four questions
 
 1. **Intent.** Is the thing called a defect a deliberate choice? Look for an explicit
    override (`dir="ltr"`, `!important`, a pinned version, a forced flag), a suppression or
    exemption (a lint disable, a `@ts-expect-error` with a reason, an allowlist entry), a
    comment or commit message giving a reason (`git log -L <start>,<end>:<file>`, `git blame`, `git show <sha>`
    where your host gives you git; on keryx shell, the history excerpts the caller passes in `context_files`), and
    sibling code doing the same. A signal does not prove the choice right; it proves someone chose, so the finding has to show their reason wrong.

 review's own commands without a prompt — see

**An unrecognised option is refused, not ignored**, and the command exits 1. A
 flag that is silently dropped writes nothing and still reports success.
 
 `--head <sha>` is the commit the round ran against, written to
 `manifest.target.head` and read by the `review` completion gate — which refuses
 to complete a flow whose last round cannot say which tree it read. Omitted, it
 is `git rev-parse HEAD`: the tree the reviewers actually read, preferred over a
 `pr` target's own head so that a round run against something other than what
 will merge *fails* the gate instead of passing it. With no checkout to ask and a
 `pr` target, the pull request's head is used instead; with neither, the head is
 left off and the gate reports it as unobserved.
 
 `review complete --head <sha>` names the commit the round actually reviewed when the one recorded
 at start is wrong or missing. The completion gate then checks that commit and the closed manifest
 records it (with a warning when it replaces a different recorded head). The gate is not loosened: a
 head that is not the pull request's head still needs the first line of `report.md` to name it and
 say the PR moved, and the SHA must be 7-40 hex characters on a package bound to a pull request.
 
 A package is bound to a pull request when it targets one or when its `--ref` is a pull request URL, whatever `--target` was typed: `review ingest --target report --ref <PR URL>` gets the same check, so a head recorded at ingest that is no longer the PR's head cannot close a package unchecked.

 ### Premise — `--premises`
 
 `ingest` also accepts the output of the `review-premise` skill, run after the verifier over the canonical findings. A finding can reproduce and still be no defect: the code may carry an explicit override, an exemption note or a sibling doing the same, and accepted platform practice may support it. The judge answers `upheld`, `downgraded`, `challenged` or `owner-decision` per finding. **The merge can only hold or lower.** It never adds a finding, raises a severity or edits a finding's text, and it never dismisses one: `challenged` and `owner-decision` hold the finding for the operator, who answers with `keryx review decide-premise`. A held finding is not an open blocker or major, is listed as "awaiting operator", and fails readiness and the flow review gate until it has an answer.

 ### A finding points at the code it quotes
 
 A finding does not report a line number. It reports `quote` — the code it is
 about, copied out of `file` — and `review ingest` locates that quote at the
 commit the round records, writing the line the match started on. `line` is
 therefore **output**, and a number a reviewer puts there is overwritten.
 
 The reason is the failure it replaces: nothing compared a reported line to
 anything, so a number that had drifted travelled into `findings.json`, into the
 report, and into the disposition somebody later recorded against it. On a fix
 round the file has moved under the finding by construction, which is when the
 reported number is least trustworthy and most acted upon.
 
 Matching is exact first, then with whitespace collapsed, then it stops — nothing
